description: We are a team of passionate innovators, developers and problem-solvers at Periapsys, driven by curiosity and a common vision to make a meaningful impact using technology. We’re leveraging our passions for space science, geospatial intelligence and software development to convert complex Earth-observation data into useful insights. With SAAR we aim to make industrial development smarter, informed and environmentally-responsible.
summary:
We developed GeoSARvice, an Earth Observation and Geospatial Machine Learning platform that makes industrial site selection smarter, faster, and more reliable. It combines NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) L-band data, satellite observations, geospatial analysis, and machine learning to assess ground stability, monitor environmental changes, and identify suitable industrial locations.

Traditional site selection depends on outdated maps, historical records, and manual surveys, making it time-consuming and costly. GeoSARvice addresses these challenges using NISAR's 12-day observation cycle and all-weather radar technology, which operates day and night, even through clouds. Under suitable conditions, it can detect ground movements at millimetre-scale precision.

The platform integrates radar data with terrain, climate, vegetation, and infrastructure information into a 1 km × 1 km grid to generate suitability scores and rankings.

Tested across five Indian industrial corridors—Dholera, Sanand-Viramgam, Vadodara, Bhiwadi-Neemrana, and Ludhiana—it analysed 11,382 grid cells, filtered 8,006 unsuitable cells, and identified 3,376 potential locations, achieving a maximum suitability score of 91.4/100.

With time-series visualisations, deformation animations, and confidence-rated reports, GeoSARvice supports informed decision-making, reduces development risks, and promotes sustainable industrial growth.
details:
What does GeoSAR do?

GeoSARvice is a geospatial decision‑support application for large‑scale sustainable industrial site selection. Specifically:

1. Tracks surface motion: GeoSARvice uses the NISAR L‑band repeat‑pass Interferometric SAR to measure how the ground moves in the line of sight its speed and seasonal changes every twelve days.

2. Fuses earth observations: GeoSARvice pulls together thirty‑eight features from six open satellite and geospatial sources and places them on a single 1 km by 1 km Albers equal‑area grid that covers eleven thousand three hundred eighty‑two cells in five study areas.

3. Scores and ranks sites on the fly: GeoSARvice checks each cell for nine factors—ground stability, water availability, power, transport, environment, vegetation, settlements, climate and terrain—and lets users choose from sixteen ready‑made industry profiles or change the importance of each factor while they work.

4. Forecasts short‑term trends and oddities: GeoSARvice picks the temporal model for each factor to predict conditions four months ahead also offering 3, 5 and 10 year outlooks and it highlights statistical oddities using unsupervised group methods.

5. Shows radar evidence and uncertainty: GeoSARvice offers a moving surface animation multiple map layers, a comparison, a scenario lab and automatic site briefs that clearly show site quality, versus data confidence never guessing missing data.

 

How does it work?

The platform operates through a five-stage computational pipeline:

1. HTTP Range-Request Data Streaming:

Instead of downloading huge 2–9 GB NISAR HDF5 archives GeoSARvice asks the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) catalogue for data and streams only the compressed HDF5 pieces that fall inside the 45 km × 45 km study area. This process is done with HTTP byte-range requests that move only 3–5% of the raw file size and platform also downloads Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover, NASA POWER MODIS NDVI and OpenStreetMap layers at the same time.

2. Backscatter Processing:

NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Unwrapped Interferograms (GUNW). Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) products are checked very carefully. The checks include a coherence threshold of least 0.35, a 3×3 multilook to a 240 m grid removal of ionospheric phase screen removal of planar orbital ramp and a Small Baseline Subset (SBAS) generalized least‑squares inversion. These steps pull out displacement time series and line‑of‑sight velocity.

3. 1 Km Equal‑Area Grid Fusion:

All radar data and other layers are put onto fixed 1 km × 1 km Albers equal‑area cells, such as IN_4778_3612. They are also lined up in time using the 12 months of data. If data is missing the value stays as NaN of being guessed. This raw state goes into a weighted geometric‑mean confidence score.

4. Adaptive Modelling & Anomaly Screening:

Hard limits automatically drop protected areas and slopes than 8 degrees. For the cells that survive a set of time models—linear, polynomial, sinusoidal, Fourier, GAM and Kalman filter—are tested against each other using rolling‑origin cross‑validation measured by RMSE and AICc. The best model is chosen by comparing its skill to a persistence baseline. Separately Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor (LOF) and robust Z‑scores look for cells that act like outliers.

5. Interactive Decision Support:

A web interface built with React and Leaflet/Cesium loads the exported JSON files. Platform calculates weighted project‑fit scores, from zero to one hundred shows Monte Carlo sensitivity ranges and plays SAR displacement animations at once.

What benefits does it have?

1. Environmental: It automatically enforces exclusions in national parks and protected ecosystems. It also penalizes development in wetlands, mangroves and areas with high-value tree cover. This helps guide growth away from ecologically sensitive areas.

2. Social: It replaces hidden methods for land selection with open audit-ready reports. These reports show uncertainty point out how close development is to communities, and require on-the-ground geotechnical checks and community consultations before any project moves forward.

3. Economic: It significantly lowers the costs of early-stage site screening. It also prevents infrastructure losses caused by problems, like land subsidence, waterlogging, heatwaves or weak power and transport connections. (e.g., proximity to >= 33kV substations, rail, and major roads).

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, our goal is to validate GeoSARvice's 1 km screening framework across our five Indian industrial corridor case studies—demonstrating how NISAR L-band interferometry and multi-source fusion can rapidly narrow 11,382 candidate cells down to actionable, confidence-scored shortlists. In the long term, as NISAR's continuous 12-day observation archive grows, we aim to integrate both ascending and descending passes (to decompose 3D vertical and east-west ground motion), incorporate NISAR S-band backscatter and weather-model tropospheric corrections, and scale GeoSARvice globally into an open-source standard for climate-resilient, sustainable infrastructure planning.

 

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

· Programming Languages: Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS

· Scientific & Geospatial Processing: NumPy, SciPy, pandas, h5py, pyproj, rasterio, Shapely, scikit-image, SNAPHU (phase unwrapping), NetworkX, PyYAML

· Machine Learning & Statistical Modeling: scikit-learn (Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor, Gradient Boosting, HistGradientBoostingRegressor), NumPy (generalized least squares SBAS inversion, rolling-origin cross-validation, Monte Carlo uncertainty)  

· Data Access: asf_search, NASA Earthdata Login, NASA POWER API, ORNL DAAC MODIS Web Service, Overpass API, AWS Open Data

· Frontend & Interactive Mapping: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Recharts, Framer Motion, Zustand, TanStack Query

· AI for Interpretation: Google Gemini API (gemini)

Data Formats & Storage Architecture: HDF5 (chunked HTTP range streaming), GeoTIFF, compressed NumPy archives (.npz), Parquet, CSV, JSON, GeoJSON, SHA-256 checksum manifests

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

  Gemini: Utilised for advanced data interpretation, synthesis of multi-source research, and structuring presentation deliverables.

 ChatGPT: Employed for creative brainstorming, environmental framing, and initial conceptualisation.

  Claude: Used for robust Python code generation, algorithm implementation, and technical problem-solving.

  AI Design Tools: Leveraged to generate and refine the project logo and visual assets
